title: Taking a fraction of a fraction
objectives: Multiply two fractions with an area model
Explain why the product of two fractions less than one is smaller than both
Find a fraction of a fraction of a sum of money

screens.prose: Half a bar is left on the plate: the shaded half. You eat half of what is left. The dashed lines cut each half in two.
screens.question: How much of the whole bar do you eat?

options.why: You ate half of the whole bar. You ate half of the half that was left.
You added a half and a half. "Half of" takes a part of the leftover; it is not an extra half.

hints.text: What is the shaded half cut into?
The dashed line cuts the leftover half in two.
Half of a half is one of the 4 equal pieces of the whole bar.

feedback.correct: Half of a half is a quarter of the bar.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at how much of the whole bar one piece of the shaded half is.

explain.text: You took half of the leftover half. The dashed lines split the bar into 4 equal pieces, and you ate 1 of them. So half of a half is $\tfrac{1}{4}$.

screens.prose: This bar is cut into 3 rows and 4 columns. The 3 shaded columns are $\tfrac{3}{4}$ of the bar. You eat $\tfrac{2}{3}$ of the shaded part. Tap a piece to pick it.
screens.question: Pick the pieces you eat, using whole rows from the top.

hints.text: The shaded part has 3 rows. How many rows is two thirds of it?
This is the shaded part you eat from.
Take the top 2 rows of the shaded columns: 2 rows of 3 pieces.

feedback.correct: Two of the three rows of the shaded part.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Stay inside the shaded columns and take 2 of their 3 rows.

byKey.whole-rows: You took two thirds of the whole bar. You only eat from the shaded three quarters.
byKey.one-row: You took one row of the three. Two thirds is 2 of the 3 rows.
byKey.all-shaded: You picked the whole shaded part. You eat two thirds of it, not all of it.
byKey.c14: That piece is outside the shaded part, so it is not yours to eat.
byKey.c24: That piece is outside the shaded part, so it is not yours to eat.
byKey.c34: That piece is outside the shaded part, so it is not yours to eat.

explain.text: You ate 2 of the 3 rows inside the shaded columns: 6 small pieces. The whole bar has 12, so you ate $\tfrac{6}{12}$ of the bar. That is $\tfrac{1}{2}$ of the bar.

screens.prose: Taking $\tfrac{2}{3}$ **of** $\tfrac{3}{4}$ is called **multiplying**, written $\tfrac{2}{3} \times \tfrac{3}{4}$. Here a new bar shows $\tfrac{3}{5}$ in solid columns. The hatched part takes $\tfrac{1}{2}$ of it: the top row.
screens.question: What is $\tfrac{1}{2} \times \tfrac{3}{5}$, as a fraction of the whole bar?

hints.text: How many small pieces are in the whole bar?
These are the hatched pieces: half of the solid part.
Three hatched pieces out of 10 in the whole bar.

feedback.correct: Three of the ten small pieces.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the hatched pieces, and every piece in the whole bar.

byKey.tops-bottoms: You added the tops and the bottoms. Count the hatched pieces against the whole bar instead.
byKey.sum: You added a half and three fifths. "Of" takes a part of the solid part, so the answer is smaller.
byKey.kept: That is the solid three fifths. Only half of it is taken.
byKey.half: You gave the half on its own. Count the hatched pieces against the whole bar of 10.

explain.text: You counted 3 hatched pieces out of 10, so $\tfrac{1}{2} \times \tfrac{3}{5} = \tfrac{3}{10}$. On top, $1 \times 3 = 3$; on the bottom, $2 \times 5 = 10$. The grid made the tops multiply and the bottoms multiply.

screens.prose: You took $\tfrac{2}{3}$ of $\tfrac{3}{4}$ and got $\tfrac{6}{12}$. Now swap them. The solid columns are $\tfrac{2}{3}$ of this bar. The hatched part takes $\tfrac{3}{4}$ of it: 3 of the 4 rows.
screens.question: How does $\tfrac{3}{4}$ of $\tfrac{2}{3}$ compare with $\tfrac{2}{3}$ of $\tfrac{3}{4}$?

options.why: You expected taking three quarters to leave more. Count the hatched pieces: 6 of 12, as before.
You expected starting from the smaller $\tfrac{2}{3}$ to give less. The hatched part is still 6 of 12 pieces.

hints.text: Count the hatched pieces and the pieces in the whole.
These are the hatched pieces.
Six hatched pieces of 12, the same as last time.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the hatched pieces out of the whole bar.

explain.text: You counted 6 hatched pieces out of 12 again. Swapping the order just turns the rectangle on its side. So $\tfrac{3}{4} \times \tfrac{2}{3} = \tfrac{2}{3} \times \tfrac{3}{4}$.

screens.prose: Now take a fraction of more than one whole. You have 2 bars of chocolate, side by side. You give away $\tfrac{3}{4}$ of them: the shaded rows.

state.caption: Each bar is cut into 4 quarters

screens.question: How many bars of chocolate do you give away?

hints.text: How many quarters are shaded in each bar?
Bar 1 alone has these 3 shaded quarters.
Each bar gives 3 quarters. Two bars give 6 quarters, and 4 quarters make one bar.

feedback.correct: Six quarters: one and a half bars.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the shaded quarters, then turn them into bars.

byKey.pair-whole: That is the share of the pair. The question asks how many bars, and each bar is 4 quarters.
byKey.pieces: You counted the shaded pieces. Each piece is a quarter of a bar.

explain.text: You gave away 3 quarters of each bar: 6 quarters, or $1\tfrac{1}{2}$ bars. So $\tfrac{3}{4} \times 2 = \tfrac{6}{4}$. That is less than the 2 bars you had, but more than $\tfrac{3}{4}$.

screens.prose: With whole numbers, multiplying makes things bigger: $3 \times 4 = 12$. Now look at $\tfrac{1}{2} \times \tfrac{4}{5}$. The solid row is $\tfrac{1}{2}$ and the hatched columns are $\tfrac{4}{5}$.
screens.question: Which is true about $\tfrac{1}{2} \times \tfrac{4}{5}$?

options.text: It is bigger than both $\tfrac{1}{2}$ and $\tfrac{4}{5}$
options.why: You expected multiplying to make things bigger, as with whole numbers. Taking a part of a part gives less.
You expected it to land between the two. It is half of $\tfrac{4}{5}$, which is $\tfrac{2}{5}$, below $\tfrac{1}{2}$ too.

hints.text: Is half of something more or less than that something?
The pieces that are solid and hatched are half of the four fifths.
Solid and hatched: 4 of 10 pieces, which is $\tfrac{2}{5}$. That is less than $\tfrac{1}{2}$ and less than $\tfrac{4}{5}$.

feedback.correct: Four tenths is less than a half and less than four fifths.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the pieces that are both solid and hatched.

byKey.bigger: You carried "multiplying makes bigger" over from whole numbers. With two amounts less than one, you take a part of a part.

explain.text: You found $\tfrac{4}{10} = \tfrac{2}{5}$, smaller than both. Half of four fifths must be less than four fifths. And four fifths is less than a whole, so half of it is less than a half.

screens.prose: In every grid, the pieces in both shadings were top times top. The whole was bottom times bottom. $$\frac{2}{3} \times \frac{3}{4} = \frac{2 \times 3}{3 \times 4} = \frac{6}{12}$$ Multiply the tops to count the shared pieces. Multiply the bottoms to count the whole.
screens.question: What is $\tfrac{2}{5} \times \tfrac{3}{4}$?

options.why: You added the tops and the bottoms. "Of" multiplies them.
You multiplied across, 2 by 4 and 5 by 3. Multiply top by top and bottom by bottom.
You added the two fractions. Taking $\tfrac{2}{5}$ of $\tfrac{3}{4}$ gives less than $\tfrac{3}{4}$.

hints.text: What did the shared pieces count in the grids?
Tops: $2 \times 3 = 6$. Bottoms: $5 \times 4 = 20$.

feedback.correct: Top times top, bottom times bottom.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the tops together and the bottoms together.

explain.text: A grid of 5 rows by 4 columns has 20 pieces. Two rows of three columns share 6 of them. So $\tfrac{2}{5} \times \tfrac{3}{4} = \tfrac{6}{20}$, which is also $\tfrac{3}{10}$.

screens.prose: Put the lines in order to show why $\tfrac{2}{5}$ of $\tfrac{3}{4}$ is $\tfrac{6}{20}$.
screens.question: Put the lines in order.

lines.text: Cut the bar into 4 columns and shade 3: that is $\tfrac{3}{4}$.
Cut every column into 5 rows, so the whole bar has $4 \times 5 = 20$ pieces.
Take 2 of the 5 rows inside the shaded columns: $2 \times 3 = 6$ pieces.

hints.text: What has to exist before you can take two fifths of it?
The rows must be cut before you can take 2 of them.
Shade the columns, cut the rows, take the rows, conclude.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what each line needs from the lines before it.

byKey.take: You took rows before cutting them. The 5 rows exist only after the cut.
byKey.rows: Cutting rows comes after the bar shows $\tfrac{3}{4}$, the amount we take a part of.

explain.text: The three quarters must be shaded first, then cut into rows, then 2 rows taken. Counting gives 6 pieces of 20. Each count is a product, which is why the rule multiplies.

screens.prose: You own $\tfrac{1}{4}$ of a small trading firm. This year it made £1,200 profit. It paid $\tfrac{2}{3}$ of the profit out to its owners and kept the rest.

state.caption: Solid: the $\tfrac{2}{3}$ paid out. Hatched: your $\tfrac{1}{4}$ of it

screens.question: How much of the profit is paid to you, in pounds?

hints.text: First find the payout, then your quarter of it.
The hatched pieces are your quarter of the paid-out rows.
$\tfrac{1}{4} \times \tfrac{2}{3} = \tfrac{2}{12}$. Each twelfth is £100, so you get £200.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the payout first, then take your quarter of it.

byKey.no-payout: That is a quarter of all the profit. Only the $\tfrac{2}{3}$ paid out goes to owners.
byKey.payout: That is the whole payout. You own a quarter of it.
byKey.added: You added $\tfrac{1}{4}$ and $\tfrac{2}{3}$. You get a quarter of two thirds, so multiply.

explain.text: The firm paid out $\tfrac{2}{3}$ of £1,200, which is £800. Your quarter of that is £200: $\tfrac{1}{4} \times \tfrac{2}{3} = \tfrac{2}{12}$ of the profit. Each twelfth is £100, and 2 are hatched.

ideas: Taking a fraction of a fraction is multiplying. Cut one way for the first fraction and the other way for the second.
The shared pieces count top times top; the whole counts bottom times bottom.
A part of a part is smaller than either part. Multiplying makes bigger only when a number is more than one.

formula.name: Multiplying fractions
formula.note: Read $\times$ as "of": $\tfrac{1}{4} \times \tfrac{2}{3}$ is a quarter of two thirds.

summary.trap: Multiplying does not always make bigger. $\tfrac{1}{2} \times \tfrac{4}{5} = \tfrac{2}{5}$, less than both.

options.why: You added the tops and the bottoms. Taking a third of a half multiplies them.
You added a third and a half. A third of a half is less than a half.

feedback.correct: A third of a half is a sixth.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the tops and multiply the bottoms.

explain.text: Cut a half into 3 equal parts: each is one of 6 equal pieces of the whole. So $\tfrac{1}{3} \times \tfrac{1}{2} = \tfrac{1}{6}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find one fifth of £20 first.

byKey.one-fifth: That is one fifth of £20. You need 3 of them.
byKey.times: You multiplied £20 by 3 without splitting it into fifths first.

explain.text: One fifth of £20 is £4. Three fifths is $3 \times £4 = £12$. In the rule, $\tfrac{3}{5} \times 20 = \tfrac{60}{5} = 12$.

options.why: You added the tops and the bottoms. "Of" multiplies them.
You multiplied the tops but kept the bottom as 5. The bottoms multiply too: $3 \times 5 = 15$.

feedback.correct: All of two fifths is two fifths.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. What is $\tfrac{3}{3}$ as an amount?

explain.text: Three thirds is one whole, so you take all of $\tfrac{2}{5}$. The rule agrees: $\tfrac{3 \times 2}{3 \times 5} = \tfrac{6}{15} = \tfrac{2}{5}$.

options.why: You expected multiplying by a half to leave a half alone or grow it. Half of a half is a quarter.
You expected any multiplying to shrink a half. Times 2 doubles it to 1.

feedback.correct: Half of a half is a quarter.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out each amount.

explain.text: The three amounts are $\tfrac{1}{4}$, $\tfrac{1}{2}$ and $1$. Multiplying by a fraction less than one shrinks; multiplying by 2 doubles.
